title: Trump Uses Rare 'Pocket Rescission' to Cut $1 Billion Congress Already Approved
summary:
President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending that Congress already approved — using a rare and contested power called a "pocket rescission" (when a president cancels funding and gives Congress almost no time to respond).

The White House announced the cuts Friday. Most target Health and Human Services programs serving refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the money isn't needed because illegal border crossings have dropped considerably. Also cut: a Department of Education program for migrant students, a Justice Department office focused on reducing racial tensions, a minority business development initiative, HUD housing counseling, and HHS grants the administration called "outright harmful and blatantly ideological." A White House press release notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic President Barack Obama.

The list goes further. The White House said it is also rescinding $70 million for what it called "woke" international education programs, $28 million in HHS research grants, $9 million in debt relief for foreign countries that fund climate change policies, and $10 million from a minority business development program.

Even a Republican is objecting. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, said the action came "without warning or consultation." She called it "a usurpation of Congress's appropriations powers" and said OMB "does not get to decide which programs are worth funding." Collins added that she would work with colleagues to address "these illegal actions."

Here's the catch: federal law gives Congress 45 days to review proposed cuts. Trump announced them with only five days left in the fiscal year — and the House is out of session through November. The Government Accountability Office, an arm of Congress, says the maneuver is illegal.

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the committee, called it "theft from the American people, plain and simple." She said Republicans have declined to back language preventing the administration from usurping Congress's spending power.

This isn't the first time. A year ago, Trump issued the first pocket rescission in nearly 50 years, blocking $4.9 billion in foreign aid. The Supreme Court declined to block it, citing presidential authority over foreign affairs. This time, the target is domestic spending — and the fight over who controls the federal purse is heading to the courts.
why_it_matters: This is a live test of the separation of powers: if a president can effectively cancel spending lawmakers approved, Congress's constitutional 'power of the purse' becomes much weaker, setting a precedent that future presidents of either party could use.

background_read: This fight has a long history. After President Richard Nixon tried to refuse to spend money Congress had approved, lawmakers passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which says a president who wants to cancel spending must formally ask Congress — and Congress then gets 45 days to approve or reject the request.
A 'pocket rescission' exploits the timing of that rule. If the request arrives so late in the fiscal year that Congress cannot realistically finish reviewing it, the money may simply never be spent.

The office at the center of the argument is the Office of Management and Budget, or OMB — the White House office that writes the president's budget and oversees how federal agencies spend their money. Sen. Susan Collins (a Republican from Maine who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, the panel that writes spending bills) said OMB 'does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.'

Under the U.S. Constitution, Congress holds the 'power of the purse': only lawmakers can decide how federal money is raised and spent, and the executive branch is supposed to carry those decisions out.

The Government Accountability Office (Congress's own watchdog, which audits federal spending) has said the earlier version of this maneuver was illegal. With this year's cuts aimed at domestic programs rather than foreign aid, the dispute over who controls the federal purse now appears headed to the courts.

perspectives.description: The White House argues the money is unnecessary because illegal border crossings have fallen sharply, and that some grants are 'outright harmful and blatantly ideological.' From this angle, the cuts save taxpayer money and reassert presidential control over how agencies spend.

perspectives.perspective: Negative: bipartisan concern about Congress's power
perspectives.description: Even a Republican committee chair, Susan Collins, calls the move an 'usurpation' made 'without warning or consultation,' while Democrat Patty Murray calls it 'theft.' Their shared worry is that the 45-day review the law requires became impossible, so Congress was cut out of decisions it is supposed to make.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral/analytical: a loophole meeting an old law
perspectives.description: The Impoundment Control Act was written in 1974 after Richard Nixon refused to spend approved funds. Every president since has worked within it, and the law's 45-day clock assumes a request arrives early enough to be reviewed — a timing rule this maneuver deliberately strains.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: what the courts and future presidents do next
perspectives.description: Because the targets are domestic programs this time, not foreign aid, the Supreme Court's earlier reasoning about foreign affairs may not carry over. A court ruling could either close the timing loophole or hand future presidents a powerful new budget tool.
